question: In a recent technical brief, the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Europe warned that insufficient and inadequately skilled nursing staff are jeopardising patient safety and accelerating burnout across European healthcare systems.

According to the WHO Regional Office for Europe, staff shortages, rising care demands and increasing mental health strain are creating a ‘ticking timebomb’, with a projected shortfall of nearly one million healthcare professionals in Europe by 2030.

Nurses represent 56 % of the health workforce, yet inadequate nurse-to-patient ratios and poor workforce planning are heightening clinical risks and driving professionals out of the sector. The WHO calls for nursing care to be treated as safety-critical, alongside improved staffing standards, better management of care complexity and greater use of digital tools to reduce administrative burdens.

Given that health workforce resilience is essential to the functioning of national health systems and to EU health security more broadly, what actions does the Commission intend to take, within its competences, to support Member States in addressing nursing shortages, promoting safe staffing standards and improving retention and working conditions across the EU?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.5.2026) Nurse shortages and more broadly health workforce shortages are an important challenge, requiring action in line with the division of competences in the EU. According to Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU1, Member States are responsible for the management of health services, which includes ensuring adequate staffing levels.
The Commission supports Member States in addressing health workforce challenges, including those related to nurses, notably through knowledge sharing and technical assistance.

For example, the EU4Health Programme funds initiatives addressing workforce challenges2, including the Nursing Action3 implemented in partnership with World Health Organization/Europe, which supports countries in developing effective recruitment and retention strategies. The technical brief4 referred to by the Honourable Members is a deliverable of this EU action, highlighting participating countries’ experiences.

This work also adds to that of the Commission’s Expert Group on Health Systems Performance Assessment (HSPA)5. The group has mapped approaches to safe staffing levels across all health professions, including but not only nurses, and is foreseen to publish a report to further support the exchange of experiences.

To facilitate mobility across the EU, the Professional Qualifications Directive6 sets out the rules on recognition of professional qualifications obtained in the EU and harmonises minimum training requirements for nurses responsible for general care.
The upcoming Skills Portability Initiative7 aims at modernising and speeding up the processes for EU citizens and introducing common rules on recognition to attract talent from third countries8.
